segments.speaker: host_a
segments.text: Okay so I spent the week inside six documents about commercial fusion and I came out with one sentence: the money changed hands, and the physics did not notice.

segments.speaker: host_b
segments.text: That's a good hook. Break it down, because 'money changed hands' sounds like a press release.

segments.speaker: host_a
segments.text: Fair. The Congressional Research Service says the US fusion energy sciences budget was seven hundred ninety million dollars in fiscal 2025. Congress then appropriated about eight hundred six million for the next year.

segments.speaker: host_b
segments.text: So roughly flat, with a rounding error of optimism.

segments.speaker: host_a
segments.text: Exactly. And against that, the Fusion Industry Association counted four point four eight billion dollars of private investment in the twelve months to July 2026. Fourteen point two four billion cumulative since 2021.

segments.speaker: host_b
segments.text: So the private sector is now outspending the public programme by a factor of five in a single year. That is the actual news.

segments.speaker: host_a
segments.text: There is a catch though. The CRS runs its own survey and gets nearly nine billion cumulative for 2021 to 2025. Same direction, half the total. They are counting different things.

segments.speaker: host_b
segments.text: Which is the sort of detail that decides whether a number is a fact or a slide.

segments.speaker: host_a
segments.text: Now the machine. ITER lowered its sixth sector module into the pit on the twenty-eighth of July 2026. Roughly eleven hundred tonnes, a thirty hour lift, and two thirds of the torus is now in place.

segments.speaker: host_b
segments.text: And that is ahead of schedule, right? I remember ITER being a synonym for delay.

segments.speaker: host_a
segments.text: About six months ahead on this campaign. The ninth module is planned for 2027. What improved is the assembly process, not the plasma physics.

segments.speaker: host_b
segments.text: So the part you can schedule got better. What about the part you can't?

segments.speaker: host_a
segments.text: Three things keep showing up. Structural materials that survive fourteen mega electron volt neutrons. A breeding blanket that makes its own tritium. And a supply chain that can qualify either one at scale.

segments.speaker: host_b
segments.text: And tritium is the quiet killer, isn't it? Civil inventory is measured in kilograms.

segments.speaker: host_a
segments.text: Right. Deuterium is seawater. Tritium you have to breed, in the blanket you have not built yet.

segments.speaker: host_b
segments.text: So when the roadmap says mid twenty thirties, what is it actually promising?

segments.speaker: host_a
segments.text: Pilot plants. And industry's own number for what that costs is more than a billion dollars a year for a decade. Congress appropriated seven hundred ninety million.

segments.speaker: host_b
segments.text: There's the gap, in two numbers.

segments.speaker: host_a
segments.text: And the cleanest finding in the whole set: the CRS says no defensible levelised cost figure exists yet. So anyone quoting you a price per megawatt hour is quoting a projection.

segments.speaker: host_b
segments.text: Three takeaways then?

segments.speaker: host_a
segments.text: One: private capital now sets the pace. Two: ITER's assembly is genuinely ahead, and that is an engineering win, not a commercial one. Three: materials, tritium and supply chain are unsolved and they are not on anyone's schedule.

segments.speaker: host_b
segments.text: And the thing to watch next is the 2027 appropriation, because the authorisation ceiling is a billion one and the cheque keeps coming in smaller.

segments.speaker: host_a
segments.text: That's the episode. Sources are in the notebook, citations on every claim.
